headline_en: 174 Bangladeshis arrested in Malaysia
summary_en: Malaysia's Immigration Department arrested 468 foreigners, including 174 Bangladeshis, in raids on 20 November 2025 in Cameron Highlands, Pahang. The raids covered commercial areas, construction sites and vegetable farms; those arrested are accused of holding expired passports, having no travel documents and other immigration offences, and some showed temporary work permits that appeared fake. From the start of 2025 to 18 November, 83,994 foreigners were detained across Malaysia.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Immigration Department arrested 468 foreigners, including 174 Bangladeshis, in several raids in Cameron Highlands, a tourist area in Pahang state, Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: The Cameron Highlands raids ran from 11 am to 2 pm on Thursday 20 November 2025 in four areas, covering commercial zones, building construction sites and vegetable farms; 547 Immigration Department members and officers took part and a Bernama reporter was present.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report citing Bernama

facts.statement: During the Cameron Highlands raids most of the foreigners were busy packaging vegetables; they did not notice the authorities' arrival and had no chance to flee.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report citing Bernama

facts.statement: The Cameron Highlands raids in Malaysia were planned a month in advance on the basis of various complaints from local residents.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: In the Cameron Highlands operation the details of a total of 1,886 foreigners were checked, of whom 468 were arrested.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Those arrested in Cameron Highlands, Malaysia were accused of holding expired passports, having no travel documents and other breaches of immigration law; some showed temporary work permits that appeared to be fake.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia Immigration Department, as reported

facts.statement: Nationalities of the 468 arrested in Cameron Highlands: 175 from Myanmar, 174 from Bangladesh, 67 from Indonesia, 20 from Nepal, 16 from Pakistan, 11 from India, and one each from the Philippines, Thailand, Sri Lanka, China and Colombia. They were 388 men, 76 women and 4 children.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Of those arrested in Cameron Highlands, people aged 20 to 54 will be sent to detention centres in Kelantan, Perak and Selangor, Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Malaysia's immigration chief said intelligence showed Cameron Highlands has become an attractive work hub for foreigners, with arrivals rising notably in recent years, worrying local residents; foreigners like working there because it is hilly and far from cities, and local business owners often prefer to hire them.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: According to Malaysia's Immigration Department statistics, 83,994 foreigners were detained across Malaysia from the beginning of 2025 to 18 November 2025 as part of controlling illegal immigration.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia Immigration Department statistics

headline_en: The South Korea dream: protests in Bangladesh and Vietnam's success
summary_en: An opinion piece by a Bangladeshi EPS worker in South Korea comparing Vietnamese and Bangladeshi workers and arguing that infighting among Bangladeshi workers in Korea and protests by EPS candidates in front of BOESEL discourage Korean employers and officials. He says passing the lottery and language test does not guarantee going to Korea, that a Korean circular for Bangladesh may come in one to two months, and that about 40,000 Bangladeshi EPS workers have gone to Korea.

facts.statement: In the EPS (Employment Permit System) process for South Korea, passing the lottery and the language proficiency test does not guarantee going to Korea; neither the government nor BOESEL gives such a guarantee, and the writer calls it an uncertain and long process that depends partly on luck.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says he has seen many times with his own eyes that factionalism, quarrels and fights among Bangladeshi workers in South Korea are discouraging Korean owners from hiring Bangladeshi workers; although they know Bangladeshis as hard-working, some behaviour makes them give visas to workers from other countries.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The recent protest by EPS workers in front of BOESEL in Bangladesh is not viewed well by South Korean officials and damages Bangladesh's image; a senior Korean official is quoted as saying 'Our country needs workers without complaints, not protesters.'
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club, quoting an unnamed senior Korean official

facts.statement: The writer says a Korean circular (EPS recruitment notice) for Bangladesh is likely within the next one to two months from late August 2025, and claims that if no Korean circular comes, Bangladesh's EPS system will be shut down.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says about 40,000 Bangladeshi EPS workers have gone to South Korea, and that Bangladeshi workers are going to South Korea every month.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says Vietnamese workers accept living 7-8 to a room, do not stop work for fasting or other religious reasons, work together without division by religion or region and readily eat Korean food, which makes them more reliable to Korean employers; he says Bangladeshi workers tend to live alone or with few people, religious observance sometimes interrupts work continuity, and many are unwilling to take on anyone not from their own district or village.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says Korean owners generally want a calm and cooperative work environment, and advises Bangladeshi EPS candidates to focus on making themselves qualified rather than protesting, so that others' future chances of going to Korea are not blocked.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

headline_en: Bangladeshi teenage girl rescued in Hyderabad; details of India-Bangladesh human trafficking ring emerging

facts.statement: Police in Hyderabad, India rescued a teenage girl who had been trafficked from Bangladesh and forced into prostitution; this was the fourth incident of a Bangladeshi woman being rescued in Hyderabad, with rescues made from brothels in Khairatabad, Chaderghat and Bandlaguda.

facts.statement: According to a law-enforcement official in India, women trafficked from Bangladesh enter India illegally by land or water with the help of agents at the border; the ringleaders in India and Bangladesh have a very strong network and arrange money for brokers and others.

facts.statement: Trafficked women are brought to India with the lure of a job and the promise of good pay: agents find helpless women or teenage girls in extremely poor areas of Bangladesh, persuade them to come with the promise of a better livelihood, and after arrival local identity documents are made for them and they are sent to different cities.
facts.source_in_article: an unnamed law-enforcement official

facts.statement: A police officer in India said men, women and children enter India illegally from Bangladesh because of poverty and earn a living presenting themselves as Bengali until they are caught.

facts.statement: Women trafficked from Bangladesh are sold to brokers in Indian cities including Kolkata, Delhi, Hyderabad and Mumbai; in Hyderabad the ringleaders operate actively in Attapur, Bandlaguda, Chintalmet, Himayatsagar Road and Champapet.

headline_en: Studying in Malaysia: scholarships, part-time job opportunities, apply with 3.5 in SSC/HSC
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students on higher study in Malaysia: admission requirements, top public universities, tuition ranges, intake windows, application and student-visa documents, the EMGS online visa process (VAL in 14 working days, then e-visa in 48 hours), steps after arrival, living costs, part-time work limits, scholarships and the post-study Employment Pass.

facts.statement: Malaysia has more than 200,000 foreign students, students from more than 140 countries study there each year, and Bangladesh ranks near the top by number of foreign students.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: General admission requirements for foreign students at Malaysian universities: at least 12 years of schooling for a bachelor's; a minimum CGPA of 3.50 out of 5 in SSC/HSC/O-level/A-level for bachelor's programmes; a bachelor's degree with at least CGPA 2.5 out of 4 for a master's; IELTS 6.5 (may vary by programme and university); some programmes may also need GRE or GMAT scores.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article names Malaysia's public universities as the best for low-cost higher education, led by Universiti Malaya (UM), Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM), Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM), International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Popular subjects for higher study in Malaysia listed by the article: MBA; bachelor's and master's in computer science, data science, medicine and health care, and banking and finance.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Depending on university and programme, a 3.5 to 4 year bachelor's degree in Malaysia may cost MYR 9,600 to MYR 137,500, and a 1 to 2 year master's programme may cost MYR 7,500 to MYR 12,700 (figures as printed).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Malaysian universities usually take applications in two windows: one opens in June each year with a deadline through September, and one opens in November with a deadline through February.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Basic documents for a Malaysian university application (varies by university): completed application form, high school certificate (for bachelor's), bachelor's certificate (for master's), passport-size photo, valid passport, motivation letter, English proficiency certificate (IELTS or TOEFL), and proof of application fee payment where applicable.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Documents for a Malaysia student visa application: one passport-size photo with white background (35/45 mm); the first pages of a passport with 18 months' validity (photo and personal details) plus any visa-stamped pages; acceptance/offer letter from the Malaysian university; medical report; copies of all academic records with certificates; a personal bond of MYR 750; English proficiency certificate (IELTS/TOEFL).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: A Malaysia student visa requires a personal bond of MYR 750, which is refunded at the end of the student's studies at the institution on condition that no provision of Malaysia's immigration law was violated.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Additional documents for the Malaysia student visa: an approval letter from the Malaysian university; a cover letter issued by the university stating the student's application to study there; proof of sufficient funds for study and living costs; and a pre-VAL medical report from the student's home country.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The pre-VAL (pre Visa Approval Letter) medical screening can be done in the student's home country or, if the student prefers, at a registered clinic after arriving in Malaysia; applicants to public universities must contact their own institution for pre-VAL medical screening instructions.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Bangladeshi students must apply for a student visa before coming to Malaysia; the application can be started online through EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services), or made through a representative of the chosen university or an EMGS agent.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services) is described as part of Malaysia's Ministry of Higher Education that runs all international-student operations and works as a one-stop centre for foreign students at public and private higher education institutions.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: A visa processing fee must be paid for the Malaysia student visa; the amount varies by university and programme (no figure given).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The Visa Approval Letter (VAL) for Malaysia is issued 14 working days after the application is submitted, and students can check the application status while it is processed; Bangladeshi students then need an e-visa at the time of entry to Malaysia, which the article says can be obtained within 48 hours.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: After arriving in Malaysia a student must have a medical screening at any EMGS-registered clinic within the first seven days, arrange housing, and contact the institution and EMGS to confirm academic documents are in order.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: After arrival the student collects from the university a Student Pass (a sticker placed in the passport) and an i-Kad (printed as 'আই-ক্যাড'; the identity card for foreign students in Malaysia, which confirms the legality of their stay).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article says living in Malaysia (housing, food, transport, medical, mobile and internet, bank account) may cost about USD 170 to 180 in total; the period (e.g. per month) is not stated.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Foreign students in Malaysia are allowed part-time work of at most 20 hours, during semester breaks or weekend holidays, subject to the validity of their Student Pass; applications for part-time work must be made through the student's own institution.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article advises students in Malaysia to look for work on campus first: university libraries, cafes or office reception desks often offer jobs that fit alongside study.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Support for foreign students in Malaysia includes loans, tuition fee waivers and education funds; popular scholarships named are the Malaysian Government Scholarship, Malaysia Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan, and the Malaysian International Scholarship, and many universities have their own scholarships, grants and tuition waivers.

facts.statement: To work in Malaysia after study a foreign student must first secure a job; the employer then takes full responsibility for the work permit, also known as the Employment Pass, valid for a minimum of 2 years and a maximum of 5 years; the passport should have at least 18 months' validity when applying for the work permit.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

headline_en: How to stop an artificial crisis in the dollar market
summary_en: A column on Bangladesh Bank's move to a market-based exchange rate and the role of remittance 'aggregators' (large money-transfer firms that collect remittances from small exchange houses). It says aggregators cut dollar sales after banks agreed not to pay above BDT 122.50, that they distort source-country remittance statistics, and gives remittance and exchange-rate figures.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank recently decided to leave the dollar exchange rate fully to the market to meet IMF loan conditions; at the start, bank treasury officials decided nobody would buy remittance dollars above BDT 122.50, and the central bank reportedly gave similar advice.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst, citing people concerned

facts.statement: After the exchange rate was left to the market, aggregator firms in the Middle East and Far East reduced their sales of remittance dollars and Bangladeshi banks could not buy as many dollars from them as expected; they are suspected of holding dollars to create an artificial crisis.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst, citing newspaper reports

facts.statement: Aggregators are large money-transfer companies that collect remittances or cross-border payment money from small exchange houses in different countries; over a few years they have come to control Bangladesh's remittance market, and banks are reportedly forced to buy expatriates' money at the dollar rate these firms set.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: In the first 10 months of fiscal year 2024-25 Bangladesh received USD 2,536 crore (25.36 billion) in remittances, 28 percent more than the same period of the previous fiscal year.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: Five to seven years ago Bangladesh's remittance market depended on small money exchanges with which banks had contracts; now small exchanges give dollars to aggregators, who bargain and sell to Bangladeshi banks at higher prices. Many aggregators are US-based.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: The columnist says it is alleged that the United States appears as the top source of Bangladesh's remittances largely because aggregators' money is recorded under the country that owns the aggregator; a large part of remittance shown as from the US is collected in the Middle East and elsewhere, and similarly much is shown as from the UK and the UAE, so source-country remittance statistics are unreliable.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: After the detainees' Bangladeshi citizenship was verified, the government began talks with the Myanmar authorities and the Bangladesh Embassy then arranged their repatriation; the families had submitted papers to the government a year earlier to bring them back.

headline_en: 11,450 Bangladeshis held in prisons in 31 countries
summary_en: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 1 July 2024 that 11,450 Bangladeshis are held in prisons in 31 countries, the most in Saudi Arabia (5,746) and India (1,579), and gave a country-by-country breakdown. He also said West Asia is the source of 60 percent of remittances and about 60 percent of Bangladeshi workers there are semi-skilled or unskilled.

facts.statement: 11,450 Bangladeshis are detained in prisons in 31 countries around the world.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

facts.statement: The largest number of Bangladeshi prisoners abroad is in Saudi Arabia, 5,746; India holds 1,579.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

facts.statement: Bangladeshis in prison by country: Turkey 508, Oman 420, Qatar 415, Greece 414, United Arab Emirates 404, South Africa 385, Myanmar 358.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

facts.statement: Bangladeshis in prison by country: Malaysia 219, Iraq 217, China 191, Hong Kong 122, Jordan 100, Italy 81, Maldives 70, Singapore 66, Indonesia 49, Lebanon 28, Spain 19, Brunei 16.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

facts.statement: Between 2 and 10 Bangladeshis are held in prisons in each of Japan, Portugal, Belgium, Mozambique, Thailand, Algeria, Libya, Sri Lanka, South Korea and Egypt.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

facts.statement: The Foreign Minister said West Asia is Bangladesh's main source of remittances, accounting for 60 percent; manpower export to the Middle East has doubled since 2009; and about 60 percent of Bangladeshi workers employed there are semi-skilled and unskilled.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in a written answer in parliament on 1 July 2024

headline_en: High Court asks to be told what action has been taken on mismanagement allegations
summary_en: On 30 June 2024 a High Court bench orally asked the state to find out and report what action has been taken on allegations of mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia, giving the Deputy Attorney General one week. The writ, filed by Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed, attached two 2 June newspaper reports and seeks a three-member probe committee led by an additional secretary.

facts.statement: A High Court bench of Justice Mustafa Zaman Islam and Justice S M Masud Hossain Dolon orally asked the state to find out and report what action has been taken on allegations of mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia; the court said it had heard a committee had been formed and asked what it had investigated and what action was taken. Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy asked for time and was given one week.
facts.source_in_article: High Court bench, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed a writ questioning inaction over media allegations about sending workers to Malaysia and seeking a direction to form a three-member investigation committee led by an additional secretary and to submit a report; he argued the writ himself.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: The writ attached two newspaper reports of 2 June 2024: one in a Bangla daily headlined '20,000 crore taka looted, shattering the dreams of 30,000 young men' about the Malaysian labour market, and one in an English daily saying more than 3,000 workers did not get tickets for Malaysia jobs because of mismanagement.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report, citing two unnamed dailies

facts.statement: Related Prothom Alo headlines embedded in the article state that 17,000 workers could not go to Malaysia even after getting final clearance, that people mortgaged land or sold cattle to go to Malaysia, and that the Malaysian labour market has been repeatedly closed amid repeated syndicates.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo related-story headlines

headline_en: Seven times the government-fixed amount is taken to send workers
summary_en: A short video-report blurb explaining the 'Malaysia syndicate': an arrangement in which only a small number of recruiting agencies are allowed to send workers to Malaysia. It began with 25 agencies and grew in three steps to 100; the headline says workers are charged seven times the government-fixed amount.

facts.statement: The 'Malaysia syndicate' (chokro) is an arrangement in which not all of Bangladesh's recruiting agencies are allowed to send workers to Malaysia; only a small number get the chance. It started with 25 member agencies and grew in three steps to 100.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo video report

facts.statement: According to the headline, seven times the government-fixed amount is taken from workers to send them to Malaysia; the text gives no taka figures.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo video report headline

facts.statement: The ringleaders of the Malaysia syndicate are alleged to have taken large sums of money from each recruiting agency to get its name included in the syndicate; no names are given.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo video report

headline_en: Will Bangladeshis in the UK be 'in danger'?
summary_en: A column by North South University migration researchers on the 16 May 2024 UK-Bangladesh agreement on returning Bangladeshis staying illegally in the UK. It gives figures on irregular Bangladeshi arrivals in Europe and asylum claims in the UK, explains the UK-Rwanda scheme and the 2017 EU-Bangladesh SOP on returns, and recommends steps for the Bangladesh government and High Commission.

facts.statement: On 16 May 2024 the governments of the United Kingdom and Bangladesh signed an agreement to curb illegal migration to the UK; its purpose is the safe return home of Bangladeshi migrants staying illegally in the UK.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: According to 2011 British government statistics, 451,529 Bangladeshis live in Britain as British citizens; 52 percent were born in Britain and the other 48 percent, born in Bangladesh or elsewhere, later got British citizenship through the 'family reunification' programme.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University, citing UK government statistics

facts.statement: The column says many Bangladeshis have tried to enter Europe illegally by six routes, especially across the Mediterranean; more than 40,000 Bangladeshis went to Europe illegally in 2023, of whom more than 15,000 entered Italy that year, and a large share of them recently tried to enter the UK by crossing the English Channel, many then claiming asylum.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: According to the EU's Asylum Information Database website, as cited in the column, 4,258 asylum seekers applied for 'protection status' in the UK in 2023 and about 71 percent of the applications were rejected. The sentence does not itself say these were all Bangladeshis, though the context is Bangladeshi applicants.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University, citing Asylum Information Database

facts.statement: The column says the British government, under its privacy law, does not publish any information about asylum applicants, so it is hard to tell whether applicants are political asylum seekers, visa overstayers or people who entered illegally.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The column describes the UK's agreement with Rwanda: a large share of illegal migrants arriving in the UK would be sent to Rwanda and kept there while their legal process is run from the UK, and after the legal steps they would be brought back from Rwanda to the UK. The authors say they have no adequate idea whether Bangladeshi migrants will be sent to Rwanda.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: In 2017 Bangladesh signed 'Standard Operating Procedures' (SOP) with the European Union to send back about 90,000 illegal migrants living in Europe; under it, Bangladeshi illegal migrants in Europe who do not get asylum after all legal processes are sent to Bangladesh. Rights activists said at the time the EU forced the deal by threatening visa policy measures.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The column says migration practitioners in Bangladesh had no chance to give recommendations before the UK-Bangladesh agreement was signed and nobody yet has a clear idea of its content, including whether it contains visa-related pressure provisions.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The column says Bangladesh receives more than USD 2 billion a year in remittances from migrants who went to the UK by legal and illegal routes.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The column says Bangladeshis who went to the UK illegally are in financial hardship from running application-related court cases day after day.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The authors recommend that the Bangladesh High Commission in the UK quickly set up a separate hotline or cell for irregular migrants, let them have needed documents sent from Bangladesh, and arrange access to specialist lawyers; these are recommendations, not existing services.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The column says the British government is interested in recruiting people from Bangladesh through legal channels as a way to curb illegal migration, and urges Bangladesh to sign a new agreement for this if the interest is real.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: The authors warn that many irregular migrants may be forced to return, and say they should not be harassed by Bangladeshi law-enforcement for political reasons or for having gone abroad with fake documents; they also urge a plan to use returnees' professional skills, and note Bangladesh's migration policy has no clear guidance on irregular migrants.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

facts.statement: According to a British government report cited in the column, about 174,000 people from Ukraine took shelter in Britain as refugees after the war began.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University, citing UK government report

facts.statement: The column notes that under the EU-Turkey deal the EU gave Turkey about USD 6 billion to stop refugees entering Europe (source: European Commission), and that Australia earlier sent illegal migrants to Papua New Guinea and later allowed some to stay in Australia based on their applications.
facts.source_in_article: the columnists Md. Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat of North South University

headline_en: How much longer must this burden be carried
summary_en: An editorial on Bangladesh agreeing, at Saudi Arabia's request, to renew the Bangladeshi passports of 69,000 Rohingya living in Saudi Arabia, a step the government took with the welfare of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia in mind. It says about 2.8 million Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia and questions how Rohingya obtained Bangladeshi passports when real citizens face harassment getting one.

facts.statement: According to media reports cited in the editorial, Bangladesh agreed, at the Saudi government's request, to renew the passports of 69,000 Rohingya living in Saudi Arabia who went there many years ago on Bangladeshi passports; a memorandum of understanding had earlier been signed, and Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Nasser bin Abdulaziz Al Dawood discussed it with Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan during a Dhaka visit.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing media reports

facts.statement: Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan said Saudi Arabia has promised it will not send the Rohingya back to Bangladesh even if their passports are renewed; the passports need renewing so they can stay in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan

facts.statement: The editorial says the Bangladesh government agreed to renew the Rohingya passports thinking of the welfare of Bangladeshis living in Saudi Arabia, after Saudi Arabia had been pressing for renewal.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: The editorial states that about 2.8 million (28 lakh) Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: Rohingya who fled Myanmar in the second half of the 1970s went to Saudi Arabia from Bangladesh and Pakistan; Pakistan sent them with travel documents while Bangladesh gave them passports directly. The Home Minister spoke of those who went in 1976-1979, but the editorial says many more went via Bangladesh after that and the real number exceeds 69,000.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: The editorial says genuine Bangladeshi citizens face various kinds of harassment when getting a passport, while Rohingya obtain passports easily; reports of Rohingya getting passports and national ID cards appear often, and some have been stopped at the airport while going abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

headline_en: USD 1.28 billion in remittances came in 19 days
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 1,281.5 million in remittances through banking channels in the first 19 days of April 2024, with no extra Eid surge seen this time. The article breaks the amount down by bank type and gives monthly and fiscal-year remittance figures.

facts.statement: In the first 19 days of April 2024, remittances equivalent to USD 128 crore 15 lakh came to Bangladesh through legal banking channels; although extra remittance usually comes for Eid, no such rise was seen this time.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank's updated remittance report

facts.statement: Of the USD 128 crore 15 lakh in the first 19 days of April 2024, USD 108 crore 81 lakh came through private banks, USD 11 crore through state-owned banks, USD 7 crore 90 lakh through one specialised bank, and USD 39 lakh 30 thousand through foreign banks.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank's updated remittance report

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh in 2024: January USD 210 crore, February USD 216 crore 60 lakh, March USD 199 crore 68 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report, Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh by fiscal year: 2022-23 USD 2,161 crore 7 lakh; 2021-22 USD 2,103 crore 17 lakh; 2020-21 USD 2,477 crore 77 lakh, the highest in a single fiscal year up to April 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report, Bangladesh Bank data

headline_en: BDT 30 crore a day in remittances came through bKash before Eid
summary_en: Remittances received through mobile financial service bKash can be withdrawn at BDT 7 per thousand from about 2,700 ATM booths of 19 banks, against BDT 18.60 per thousand at agents. bKash says over BDT 965 crore came from 12 March to 10 April 2024 from about one million expatriates; recipients also get the government incentive of BDT 25 per thousand.

facts.statement: Remittance money received through bKash can be withdrawn from about 2,700 ATM booths of 19 commercial banks across Bangladesh at a cost of BDT 7 per thousand, using either the bKash app or the USSD channel *247#.
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Withdrawing money from a bKash agent normally costs BDT 18.60 per thousand; from two 'priyo' (favourite) agents it costs BDT 14.90 per thousand, but at that rate a maximum of BDT 50,000 a month can be withdrawn.
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The 19 banks whose ATM booths allow low-cost withdrawal of bKash remittances: The City Bank, BRAC Bank, Jamuna Bank, Trust Bank, First Security Bank, Social Islami Bank, Mercantile Bank, Community Bank, NCC Bank, Shahjalal Islami Bank, NRB Commercial Bank, Union Bank, Midland Bank, Rupali Bank, BASIC Bank, Shimanto Bank, Bangladesh Krishi Bank (BKB), ICB Islamic Bank and Citizens Bank.
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: bKash remittance withdrawal at ATMs works through the bKash app or by dialling the USSD code *247#.
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: According to bKash, BDT 517 crore in remittances came through bKash accounts from more than 110 countries in the first 20 days of Ramadan 2024, and slightly more than BDT 965 crore came between 12 March and 10 April 2024 from about 10 lakh expatriates, which the article puts at slightly more than BDT 32 crore a day (the headline says BDT 30 crore a day).
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In 2023, BDT 6,252 crore in remittances came through bKash.
facts.source_in_article: bKash, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Relatives receiving remittances through bKash also get the government incentive of BDT 25 per thousand on remittances sent by expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: bKash officials
